c.tagline: Cool mountain retreat in the Cordilleras, the Philippines' pine-covered 'Summer Capital'.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are metered by law, though drivers may propose flat fares for trips outside downtown; insist on the meter or agree a price beforehand, and expect longer waits during Panagbenga Festival and heavy rain.

emergency.note: 911 is the Philippines' national emergency hotline, connecting to police, fire, and medical services nationwide.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Pickpocketing occurs in the crowded City Market and around Burnham Park, especially during festival crowds.

hood_desc: The commercial spine of Baguio around Session Road and Burnham Park, packed with restaurants, shops, and the public market; best for first-timers who want everything walkable.
A forested former US military base turned leisure park with pine trails, a golf course, and an eco-trail; suits travelers wanting a quiet, green retreat close to downtown.
A hillside viewpoint area overlooking the mining valleys of Benguet, lined with souvenir stalls and photo spots; suits day-trippers wanting classic Baguio views and quick shopping.

The area around Wright Park's horseback trails and The Mansion, the Philippine president's summer residence, with tree-lined streets nearby; suits travelers wanting a scenic, low-key base near Camp John Hay.

The bustling market district near Magsaysay Avenue, the center of local shopping for Cordillera produce, strawberries, and handicrafts; suits budget travelers and shoppers wanting to be in the middle of local life.
lodging: The Manor at Camp John Hay
Forest Lodge at Camp John Hay

water.note: Drink bottled or filtered water; tap water is not reliably potable.

transit.hours: Jeepneys and local buses typically run about 5:00 AM to 9:00-10:00 PM.
transit.pay: Cash paid to the driver or conductor (minimum fare around 9-12 pesos); there is no rechargeable card system.
transit.note: Baguio has no rail or formal bus rapid transit; shared jeepneys are the backbone of public transport, supplemented by taxis and ride-hailing apps like Grab.

transit.m: Bus (Victory Liner/JoyBus) Clark to Baguio, transfer via Angeles/Dau

tip.r: Tipping isn't obligatory, but rounding up or leaving 5-10% for good service at sit-down restaurants and for tour guides is appreciated.

food.name: Strawberry taho
food.desc: Warm silken tofu ladled into a cup with sago pearls and a sweet syrup made from Benguet strawberries, plus chunks of the fruit. A Baguio-only twist on taho.

places.name: Baguio Public Market
places.note: Vendors work the entrances from early morning, right by the strawberry section.

places.name: Burnham Park roving vendors
places.note: Taho sellers circle the lake and boat area; flag one down for a cup on a cold morning.

places.name: Mines View Park stalls
places.note: Souvenir strip where taho, strawberries and hot drinks are sold to viewpoint crowds.

food.name: Pinikpikan
food.desc: The Cordillera's most famous dish: native chicken cooked in a smoky broth with etag cured pork, ginger and sayote tops. Deeply savoury and ceremonial in origin.

places.name: Farmer's Daughter Restaurant
places.note: The go-to Cordilleran kitchen for pinikpikan, etag and pinuneg; handy after Tam-awan Village.

places.name: Cafe Yagam
places.note: Cordilleran heritage cafe serving highland classics alongside locally roasted coffee.

places.name: Cafe by the Ruins Dua
places.note: Long-running Baguio institution that plates highland ingredients for first-timers.

food.name: Baguio longganisa
food.desc: Short, garlicky, faintly sweet pork sausages, browned until the edges caramelise. Served for breakfast with garlic rice, egg and a dish of spiced vinegar.

places.name: Baguio Public Market
places.note: Rows of stalls selling it raw by the string, plus carinderias frying it for breakfast.

places.name: Good Taste Cafe and Restaurant
places.note: Enormous-portion, all-hours Baguio institution; the classic cheap silog breakfast.

places.name: Cafe by the Ruins Dua
places.note: Sit-down breakfast version with heirloom rice and house condiments.

food.name: Ube jam
food.desc: Thick, glossy purple yam jam cooked down with milk and sugar, sold in jars. Baguio's default edible souvenir and best eaten by the spoon or on bread.

places.name: Good Shepherd Convent
places.note: The famous nuns' shop; queues form early and jars sell out on weekends.

places.name: Mines View Park stalls
places.note: Backup source a short walk away, along with strawberry and peanut brittle jars.

places.name: Baguio Public Market
places.note: Cheaper local brands sold alongside strawberry jam and dried fruit.

food.name: Etag and pinuneg
food.desc: Highland charcuterie: etag is salt-cured, smoke-dried pork, pungent and intense; pinuneg is an Ibaloi blood sausage sauteed until crisp at the edges.

places.name: Farmer's Daughter Restaurant
places.note: Serves both alongside pinikpikan; the most straightforward place to try them.

places.name: Cafe Yagam
places.note: Cordilleran-run cafe that treats etag as a headline ingredient, not a novelty.

places.name: Baguio Public Market
places.note: Dried-goods section sells etag by the slab to take home.

food.name: Strawberry shortcake
food.desc: Soft sponge layered with cream and Benguet strawberries, a Baguio bakery staple that travels down the mountain in white boxes on every bus.

places.name: Vizco's Restaurant and Cake Shop
places.note: The city's best-known strawberry shortcake; buy a whole cake or a slice with coffee.

places.name: Baguio Public Market
places.note: Fresh strawberries by the punnet if you would rather assemble your own.

places.name: Mines View Park stalls
places.note: Strawberry everything, from fresh fruit to jam and wine, near the viewpoint.

food.name: Cordillera coffee
food.desc: Arabica grown around Sagada, Benguet and Kalinga, roasted locally and brewed strong. Bright, chocolatey and a world away from instant coffee.

places.name: Cafe Yagam
places.note: Cordilleran cafe pouring highland beans with native snacks; a local favourite, not a tourist stop.

places.name: Ili-Likha Artist Village
places.note: BenCab's bamboo-and-scrap food village with small cafes serving local roasts.

places.name: Baguio Public Market
places.note: Buy whole beans from Sagada and Benguet growers by the kilo.

food.name: Choco-late de batirol
food.desc: Thick native hot chocolate whipped to a froth with a wooden batirol whisk from tablea cacao. Rich, faintly gritty and made for Baguio's cold, misty afternoons.

places.name: Choco-late de Batirol
places.note: Garden cafe that made the drink a Baguio ritual; order it with suman rice cakes.

places.name: Cafe by the Ruins Dua
places.note: Serves tablea chocolate alongside heritage-ingredient breakfasts.

places.name: Ili-Likha Artist Village
places.note: Several stalls do tablea drinks in a sheltered, art-filled courtyard.

landmarks: Burnham Park
The city's green heart, designed by architect Daniel Burnham, where families pedal swan boats on the lagoon and bikes along shaded lanes.
Mines View Park
Baguio's classic observation deck peering over the Cordillera mountains and old Benguet mining valleys, ringed by souvenir and silver stalls.
Our Lady of the Atonement Cathedral (Baguio Cathedral)
A rose-pink twin-spired cathedral atop a hill in the city center, a beloved landmark that sheltered thousands during World War II.
The Mansion
The stately official summer residence of Philippine presidents, its ornate main gate patterned after London's Buckingham Palace.
Camp John Hay
A former American rest-and-recreation base turned pine-forest retreat, with heritage trails, the Bell House, and treetop adventures.
BenCab Museum
National Artist Benedicto Cabrera's hillside museum blending contemporary Filipino art, Cordillera artifacts, and a garden farm with valley views.
Tam-Awan Village
A reconstructed Ifugao and Kalinga hamlet on a hillside, where traditional huts, art workshops, and indigenous culture meet.
Wright Park
A pine-lined reflecting pool promenade opposite The Mansion, famous for pony rides on the aptly named horse trail below.
Session Road
Baguio's bustling main artery, climbing past cafés, bakeshops, and art deco facades, and pedestrianized for lively Sunday markets.
Philippine Military Academy
The country's West Point, whose manicured parade grounds, cadet drills, and weapon displays welcome visitors inside Fort del Pilar.

train.note: Baguio has no railway and never really had one - the narrow-gauge Benguet Railroad that once climbed part of the way up from the lowlands was abandoned early in the 20th century. Philippine National Railways (https://pnr.gov.ph/) operates only in southern Luzon and Bicol, and its Metro South Commuter line has been suspended since March 2024 for North-South Commuter Railway construction, so there is no train anywhere in northern Luzon. Everything reaches the city by road up Kennon Road, Marcos Highway or Naguilian Road, which is why the bus network is so dense.

bus.note: Buses are the way in: Victory Liner (https://www.victoryliner.com/) runs hourly from Cubao, Pasay and Caloocan in 5-7 hours for about P616, or around P999 on the non-stop deluxe service; Genesis Transport and its Joy Bus premium express run from Cubao, Pasay, Avenida and Paranaque; Dagupan Bus goes hourly from Cubao; and Philippine Rabbit serves Dau terminal in Angeles City (4-5 hours, about P306). From Clark airport, Partas departs around 17:00 and connects with Victory Liner at Sison. Most terminals in Baguio cluster along Governor Pack Road and Gov. Pack Extension, a few minutes' walk from Session Road; tickets for premium services are worth reserving online but ordinary departures are sold at the counter. There are no international coaches - the Philippines is an archipelago.

ferry.note: Baguio sits at about 1,500 m in the Cordillera, roughly 50 km inland from the sea, so it has no port and no boat services of any kind. The nearest passenger and RoRo ports are San Fernando in La Union (about 1.5-2 hours down the mountain) and Salomague in Ilocos Sur; long-distance domestic sailings run from Manila with 2GO Travel (https://travel.2go.com.ph/).

half.name: Asin Hot Springs
half.blurb: A cluster of natural sulfur hot spring pools set among pine-covered hills west of Baguio, a low-key spot for a soak.

half.name: La Trinidad Strawberry Farm
half.blurb: The salad bowl of the Philippines, a valley of terraced strawberry farms and vegetable gardens just below Baguio in Benguet province.

full.name: Mount Pulag National Park
full.blurb: The third-highest peak in the Philippines, famous for a pre-dawn sea of clouds that forms below its grassy summit.
